reference.source: Tachdjian's Pediatric Orthopaedics / Campbell's Operative Orthopaedics
clinicalPearls: A developmental osteochondrosis of the vertebral endplates producing a rigid structural kyphosis, distinct from postural round-back
Affected structures are the growth zones of the thoracic (or thoracolumbar) vertebral bodies
Typically presents in adolescence around the growth spurt and is more common than isolated postural kyphosis in this age group
Presents with a cosmetic thoracic hump that does not correct on active or passive extension, sometimes with aching back pain
The radiographic hallmark is anterior wedging of several adjacent vertebrae together with Schmorl nodes and irregular, narrowed endplates
The classic radiographic definition requires anterior wedging of three or more consecutive vertebrae, differentiating it from flexible postural kyphosis
Tight hamstrings and a compensatory lumbar lordosis are common associated findings
Management ranges from physiotherapy and bracing during growth to corrective surgery for severe, progressive or painful curves as needed
reference.pathophysiology: Scheuermann disease is an osteochondrosis affecting the ring apophyses and cartilaginous endplates of the growing vertebral bodies. Disordered endochondral ossification and mechanical stress at the vertebral growth zones impair the normal anterior growth of the vertebral bodies, so that the anterior height falls behind the posterior height and the vertebrae become wedged. Herniation of disc material through weakened endplates produces Schmorl nodes, and endplate irregularity with disc space narrowing follows. The cumulative anterior wedging of several adjacent vertebrae results in an increased, rigid thoracic (or thoracolumbar) kyphosis that, unlike postural round-back, does not correct with extension. A genetic predisposition and repetitive loading during rapid growth are thought to contribute.
additionalDifferentials: Compression fracture, including osteoporotic or traumatic
Ankylosing spondylitis or other inflammatory spondyloarthropathy
additionalInvestigations: Standing lateral spinal radiographs to measure the kyphotic angle and identify vertebral wedging
Assessment for anterior wedging of consecutive vertebrae, Schmorl nodes and endplate irregularity
Hyperextension lateral views to assess curve flexibility and rigidity
Magnetic resonance imaging where cord compromise, infection or tumour is a concern
Clinical assessment of hamstring tightness and any neurological signs
Serial imaging during growth to monitor curve progression
redFlags: Neurological signs or symptoms suggesting spinal cord compression from a severe curve or disc herniation
Constitutional symptoms, fever or night pain raising concern for infection or malignancy
Rapidly progressive kyphosis during the growth spurt
Severe pain out of proportion to the deformity prompting a search for another cause
reference.prognosis: Most adolescents have a stable curve and do well with observation, physiotherapy or bracing during growth; severe curves may progress and cause pain or cosmetic concern into adulthood, and neurological compromise is rare but important to recognise.
pitfalls: Mislabelling a rigid structural kyphosis as flexible postural round-back and under-treating it
Failing to appreciate the diagnostic requirement for wedging of several consecutive vertebrae
Overlooking neurological compromise in a severe or painful thoracic curve
Attributing all back pain to Scheuermann disease without excluding infection, fracture or tumour
management: Observe mild, non-progressive curves with serial radiographic monitoring during growth
Prescribe physiotherapy with extension-based exercises, hamstring stretching, and postural training
Apply bracing in the skeletally immature adolescent with a moderate or progressive curve to limit worsening during growth
Control back pain with simple analgesia and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs alongside activity modification
Refer for spinal fusion and instrumentation in severe, progressive, or painful curves, or where neurological compromise is present
Undertake serial imaging through the growth spurt to monitor curve progression and guide escalation
